Design and creation of a place-based wellbeing system.

paragraphs.text: Introduction to this approach

This commissioning approach fits most closely with the ‘whole system design’ commissioning aspect.  It represents the shift from thinking about care needs first, to thinking about wellbeing first, and begins with a view that the best way to deliver outcomes for the community is to start early and ‘upstream’ to the individual, families, neighbours, the community and other support wherever and as much as possible. Ideally, this is well before what is called ‘prevention and early intervention’ and is about creating the conditions for people to be healthy, resilient, and connected in their communities. It is more than just keeping people out of care; it is about establishing the environment, so people are able to have healthy lives.

As part of Leicester City Council’s Supported Living and Extra Care Housing Strategy, the council aims to provide up to 396 new units over ten years, including provision for supported living and other housing to delay entry into statutory care, replacement of sub-standard existing statutory care provision, and provision for care leavers aged 18-25. Two new developments contain a mix of working-age adults with care and support needs and older adults, and are connected. Tenants report that the mix has a positive impact, supports diversity, and that “some younger residents help the older ones with shopping etc, and some of the older ones support the younger ones who may not have family. This makes for a nice community of people who can balance each other’s strengths and needs.”

paragraphs.text: Examples of this approach in practice

Co-production to transform mental health services: A council faced high rates of psychosis, Mental Health Act admissions, acute hospital admissions, and adults in high cost residential and inpatient placements. Working with their then Clinical Commissioning Group, they tested co-production on a large scale, putting citizens at the heart of their own care. A series of storytelling and co-design sessions helped set a bold and shared vision for a system focused on prevention rather than crisis care. A resource map, brought to life by trained peer researchers telling community stories, identified that little funding was going to services designed to help people live well in their communities. Four key changes were made: a collaborative across service users, GPs, providers and commissioners to drive the change, an empowered network of providers, support agencies, statutory organisations and others with a focus on ‘living well’, a jointly-funded organisation that manages funds for those who need personalised care and personal budgets, and a hub to provide easy, integrated access to services. The result was a 32 per cent reduction in referrals to secondary care, with 500 people now supported by the network, many of whom would not have previously had any support at all. The waiting time for support in secondary care reduced from one month to one week. Professionals recognised the integral value of working with people with lived experience of mental health problems, and the initiative saved 20 per cent against an original budget of £12m.

paragraphs.text: One London borough is implementing a Dynamic Purchasing Vehicle, following some success in rough sleeping transformation and a realisation that supported living procurement was being limited by existing governance and process. A clear vision was presented to Cabinet along with progress on regularising existing contracts and other steps to get things better structured and organised internally. After a nine-month process of making the case and proceeding through decision-making, a Dynamic Purchasing Vehicle is now going out to tender which will allow much more flexible call-off of services. The process will start with supported living, then single vulnerable adult services, and move on, with learning embedded, to residential care, extra care, and shared lives, meaning that the onerous approval process does not have to be repeated, and a new fit-for-purpose commissioning process with more room for flexibility and learning can be developed.

paragraphs.text: A city council adult social care commissioning function was faced with the challenge of working in partnership across other council services and implementing the Care Act provisions which required flexible and effective commissioning. Over the course of a year, a Chartered Institute of Procurement and Supply (CIPS)-qualified commissioning lead supported a complete reorganisation with a strong commercial focus and significant upskilling. The service now has responsibility for service design, market shaping and ensuring effective supplier relationships. It also establishes the most appropriate routes to market, defining tendering procedures under the Light Touch Regime and tender evaluation methodologies. The council’s contract management function also includes management of major corporate contracts, and covers around one third of the council’s total spending. Approaches have included an award-winning, partnership-based advocacy service tender, Light Touch procurement (piloted with drug and alcohol treatment), implementation of a Dynamic Purchasing System, a new approach to voluntary sector procurement involving the creation of a single borough-wide consortium, with associates, using an outcome-based contract designed to support prevention, and brokering the sale of a vacant residential home to a new provider in order to maintain local capacity which was then block contracted to the local authority.

Effective delivery models enabling effective practice.

paragraphs.text: Introduction to this approach

This approach is paired with the ‘models and tactics’ commissioning aspect, and is about designing effective delivery models to support effective practice. It begins with a view that there are real savings and improvements to be made at the level of delivery model design. At its extremes, it can support an ideological view of how care should be delivered, but in general it considers that how the work is organised, governed, and delivered, is critical. This sees commissioners moving into, or working closely with those in, the service design space, undertaking customer journey mapping, empathy work, ‘citizen safaris’, ‘mystery shopping’ and so on, to understand the experience of care and to look for improvement opportunities at the process or organisational level.
